A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same QuantVGGT study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–H are readable and support reliable matching, including material moved between the appendices and main text.

before.justification: V1 reports original CO3Dv2 camera-pose and DTU point-map experiments, quantization and sampling ablations, and calibration and inference measurements.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds reconstruction benchmarks, Fast3R evaluation, sensitivity and robustness tests, and additional efficiency measurements.

M1.justification: V3 adds experimental mixed-precision/asymmetric variants and a QAT variant that fine-tunes the quantized model for one epoch on calibration data (Appendix C, Table 5). The principal DSFQ/NFDS procedure remains unchanged. Random Hadamard rotation was already specified in v1 Appendix B; its expanded construction does not establish a new core algorithm.

E1.justification: CO3Dv2 camera-pose and DTU point-map coverage is retained. V3 adds point-cloud reconstruction on 7-Scenes and NRGBD (Table 3), substantially extending dataset coverage. Appendix E also introduces a calibration scenario restricted to sequences whose first frame has very low similarity to subsequent frames.

E2.justification: V3 adds RepQ-ViT and AWQ to the W4A4 CO3Dv2 comparison in Table 1 and introduces a comparison against token-compression method FastVGGT in Table 7. Figures 11–13 additionally compare reconstructions against RTN and QuaRot. The original DTU comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include Fast3R evaluation, mixed-precision/asymmetric settings, one-epoch QAT, Table 5's first 200 sequences per class, calibration-size and hyperparameter sweeps, FLOPs comparison, and timing over 10–80 frames. Appendix B also changes the stated filtering parameter from T = 0.2 to p = 0.2; whether this corrects notation or reflects an executed change is unspecified.

E4.justification: V3 adds quantization-format/QAT comparisons, Hadamard and smoothing-factor sensitivity, NFDS threshold/cluster/sample-size sweeps, an inconsistent-first-frame stress test, preprocessing overhead measurements, sequence-length scaling, and qualitative baseline comparisons. The smoothing-order ablation is retained from v1 Table 6 and merged into v3 Table 4, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V3 Table 10 reports Hadamard sensitivity using three labeled random seeds, adding information about a separate source of variability. The five-seed sampling experiments and their reported means and variances in Figures 5 and 8 remain unchanged. No new confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Matched original CO3Dv2 and DTU scores remain unchanged; W6A6 results move into Table 1. Substantial new results cover additional datasets, models, baselines, configurations, and robustness tests. For example, Table 6 reports Fast3R mean accuracy of 0.049 for both full precision and QuantVGGT, while Table 15 reports speedups from 2.47x to 2.55x across sequence lengths. These are additions, not same-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces v1's unnormalized sign-matrix description, which nevertheless asserted orthogonality, with an explicitly normalized recursive Hadamard construction and randomized diagonal signs. This corrects a mathematical-definition inconsistency. Theorem 3.2 gains symbol explanations, but its substantive statement and Appendix A proof remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: the first VGGT-specific PTQ framework, DSFQ and NFDS contributions, strong low-bit accuracy, and approximately 3.7x memory reduction and 2.5x acceleration. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: V3 adds specific interpretations concerning transfer across architectures and quantization formats, complementarity with token merging, and robustness to inconsistent first frames through filtering and relative-frame geometry. It also discusses QAT's accuracy–cost tradeoff. These extend applicability and mechanism discussion while retaining the original explanations of DSFQ and NFDS.

D1.justification: V3 specifies RTX 4090 24GB hardware, CUDA 12.4, and CUTLASS/PyTorch for efficiency measurements, and explains CUDA Hadamard execution, LayerNorm fusion, and static versus dynamic activation quantization. V1 already supplied calibration counts, learning rates, and blockwise calibration details. The code URL and release statements are unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds references including RepQ-ViT, AWQ, FastVGGT, CUTLASS, and additional quantization and 3D research. Appendix C newly positions quantization as complementary to token compression. The main related-work narrative and VGGT-specific novelty claim remain intact; publication updates to existing references are not new works.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section organization are retained. V3 expands selected mathematical and implementation explanations, moves the smoothing-order discussion into the main text, updates affiliations and publication headers, and adds acknowledgements. This is localized editing and expansion rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the experimental displays with new benchmark, sensitivity, robustness, and efficiency tables and Figures 11–13. Table 1 incorporates the former appendix W6A6 table, and Table 4 consolidates architecture ablations. Figure 4 gains clearer labels and captions, while Figure 6 changes its latency axis from normalized units to seconds.

improvement.justification: V1's evidence centered on one backbone and lacked direct hyperparameter and first-frame stress tests. V3 adds indoor-dataset and Fast3R transfer results plus targeted sensitivity and robustness checks (Tables 3, 6, and 10–12), substantially strengthening the empirical basis for generalization and calibration stability. Deployment details also improve reproducibility. Some new settings, particularly the mixed-precision policy and evaluation subsets for Tables 11–12, remain insufficiently specified, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger validation.
